Compute Efficiency and Serial Runtime Tradeoffs
for Stochastic Momentum Methods

Depen Morwani Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute at Harvard University    Alexandru Meterez Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute at Harvard University    Pranav Ajit Nair Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute at Harvard University    Sham Kakade Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Kempner Institute at Harvard University
Abstract

Stochastic momentum methods such as heavy ball (HB), Nesterov momentum, and variants of Accelerated SGD (ASGD) (Kidambi et al., 2018) are widely used in modern training, but their stochastic benefits depend on two distinct quantities: serial runtime, the number of iterations needed to reach a target accuracy, and compute efficiency (CE), the inverse total gradient-query or FLOP cost. Larger batches reduce serial runtime without hurting CE only when the contraction gap grows linearly with batch size.

We study stochastic HB and ASGD for consistent linear regression with Gaussian covariates and prove finite-dimensional, discrete-time lower bounds on their batch-size tradeoffs. Our first result shows that HB does not improve the CE frontier over SGD for arbitrary spectra; rather, it preserves SGD-level CE over a larger batch-size window, allowing larger batches to reduce serial runtime until HB reaches its deterministic accelerated scale. This window can be a factor κ\sqrt{\kappa} larger than the SGD critical batch size. For ASGD, the picture is more spectrum-dependent: for rapidly decaying power-law spectra, ASGD improves small-batch CE over HB/SGD, but as batch size grows it trades this CE advantage for improved serial runtime. Synthetic linear-regression experiments verify these qualitative regimes, including near-overlap of ASGD and HB for slowly decaying spectra and the predicted CE–serial tradeoff for rapidly decaying spectra.

1 Introduction

††footnotetext: ∗: Equal contribution.
†\dagger: Work done while at Harvard.

Training deep neural networks is typically done via a first order optimization method, such as gradient descent (GD), or in the case of large scale datasets and models that are memory prohibitive through minibatch Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) (Robbins and Monro, 1951), with the latter method taking gradient steps on a random subsample of the population. While most open source large scale models (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) are trained with preconditioned SGD, typically Adam variants (Kingma and Ba, 2014; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017; Vyas et al., 2024), or the more recent approximate second order methods (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Gupta et al., 2018; Jordan et al., 2024), they all generally bake in a version of momentum. Assuming a noiseless quadratic model, under exact gradients classical momentum methods such as heavy ball (Polyak, 1964) and Nesterov’s accelerated gradient (Nesterov, 1983; Nesterov, 2013) improve over the GD rate of 𝒪⁡(κ)\mathcal{O}(\kappa) to 𝒪⁡(κ)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}). However, this acceleration does not extend to the stochastic regime (Kidambi et al., 2018), limiting their practicality for current training regimes.

Empirically, several works have found that momentum primarily accelerates in the large batch size regime, while in the small batch case its effects vanish (Shallue et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2023; Kunstner et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019). Most recently, Marek et al. (2025) conducted a large scale empirical study in large language model (LLM) pretraining, and have found that at small batch sizes momentum does not bring any benefits over SGD. These works indicate a subtle interplay between compute efficiency and serial runtime in stochastic acceleration. Theoretically, there has been partial progress in understanding stochastic momentum at batch size 11, through the lower bounds established by Kidambi et al. (2018) and the asymptotic characterization of Lee et al. (2022); Ferbach et al. (2025). We refer the reader to Section 2 where we discuss these works further. Based on the the theoretical understanding, new momentum schemes have been proposed combining multiple momentum buffers that provably achieve acceleration at batch size 11 (Jain et al., 2018; Vaswani et al., 2019; Liu and Belkin, 2018; Gupta et al., 2024; Ferbach et al., 2025; Pagliardini et al., 2024), a family of methods we will refer to as Accelerated SGD (ASGD) (Kidambi et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2018; Ferbach et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2022). While these methods achieve accelerated rates and thus better compute efficiency at batch size 11, this regime is far from practical from a serial runtime point of view, especially in the current pretraining setups where the number of tokens can scale to several trillions.

Thus, in large-scale pretraining, the key question is not only whether an optimizer improves sample complexity, but also whether it can maintain those gains at the large batch sizes needed to reduce serial training time. While keeping the data size fixed, one can linearly increase the batch size until the critical batch size (CBS) (Zhang et al., 2024; Shallue et al., 2019; Merrill et al., 2025; Meterez et al., 2025b) while achieving a linear decrease in the serial cost. While the CBS for SGD has been extensively studied empirically and theoretically in linear regression, to the best of our knowledge there are no results on the CBS of momentum algorithms. In this paper we provide a nearly full characterization of the serial runtime tradeoffs by providing lower bounds for arbitrary spectra for heavy ball, and power law spectra for ASGD.

1.1 Contributions

In the deterministic, full-batch regime, the classical story is clear: on a κ\kappa-conditioned quadratic, GD has contraction gap of order κ−1\kappa^{-1}, while HB achieves the accelerated gap of order κ−1/2\kappa^{-1/2}. Equivalently, HB reduces the number of serial iterations by a factor of order κ\sqrt{\kappa}. Our goal is to understand what remains of this acceleration in the stochastic mini-batch regime, where we care about both the serial runtime and the compute efficiency.

A useful way to compare stochastic momentum methods is to separate these two quantities. For a given algorithm, let s∗​(H,B)s^{*}(H,B) denote the best-achievable spectral radius, or contraction factor, at batch size BB and with covariance spectrum HH (suppressing dependence on the algorithm). We define the corresponding contraction gap by

α⁡(B):=1−s∗​(H,B).\alpha(B):=1-s^{*}(H,B).

In the full-batch limit, this gap satisfies αGD​(∞)≍κ−1\alpha_{\mathrm{GD}}(\infty)\asymp\kappa^{-1} and αHB(∞)≍κ−1/2\alpha_{\mathrm{HB}}(\infty)\asymp\kappa^{-1/2}, which is the classical deterministic acceleration of HB over GD.

The number of serial steps needed to reach a fixed target error scales as 1/α⁡(B)1/\alpha(B), while the total gradient-query cost, or total FLOPs up to constants, scales as B/α⁡(B)B/\alpha(B). Equivalently, the compute efficiency (CE) scales as

α⁡(B)B.\frac{\alpha(B)}{B}.

Thus, higher CE means fewer total FLOPs to reach a target accuracy. If α⁡(B)\alpha(B) grows linearly with BB, increasing the batch size reduces serial runtime without hurting CE. If α⁡(B)\alpha(B) grows sublinearly with BB, larger batches still improve serial runtime, but only by sacrificing CE.

Our first main result characterizes how this deterministic acceleration appears as the batch size is varied, where we compare HB to SGD, and is summarized in Table 1. The result holds for arbitrary spectra.

HB improves the serial runtime over SGD, but it does not improve the CE frontier.

More precisely, we prove a lower bound showing that HB cannot improve over the optimal CE scaling of SGD at any batch size. At small batch sizes, HB has the same linear-scaling behavior as SGD. Above the SGD critical batch size, however, HB can continue to convert larger batches into fewer serial steps while preserving the same CE scale. This continues until HB reaches its deterministic accelerated scale. Thus, HB’s benefit is not a better best-achievable CE frontier, but rather a larger batch-size window over which SGD-level CE can be used to buy improved serial runtime.

In practice, several newer stochastic momentum methods are also being considered. The majority of these schemes are paramterically equivalent to ASGD, which is known to improve CE over SGD at small batch sizes. Our second main result characterizes how this CE improvement changes with batch size.

ASGD improves small-batch CE, but its CE-preserving linear-scaling window is shorter.

We show that ASGD’s CE gains are concentrated in the small-batch regime. Unlike the case for HB, the serial-runtime picture for ASGD is more dependent on the full spectra. For rapidly decaying spectra, ASGD has an initial CE-preserving linear-scaling regime. After this regime, its contraction gap continues to improve with batch size, but only sublinearly. Thus, increasing the batch size still reduces ASGD’s serial runtime, but it does so by spending some of ASGD’s small-batch CE advantage.

More concretely, for rapidly decaying spectra, the resulting picture is as follows. At small batch sizes, ASGD has better CE than HB, consistent with known upper bounds at B=1B=1. As BB increases, ASGD moves along a CE–serial tradeoff curve: serial runtime improves, but CE decreases relative to the small-batch optimum. Eventually, ASGD reaches the deterministic accelerated serial-runtime scale. Beyond this point, further increasing the batch size no longer improves serial runtime and only decreases CE at the usual 1/B1/B rate.

Thus, ASGD improves the CE–serial frontier most strongly at small batch sizes; for larger batch sizes the advantage is more modest, because part of the small-batch CE gain has already been converted into serial-time improvement. For more slowly decaying spectra, ASGD and HB are comparable.

Figure 1 illustrates these CE–serial tradeoffs in synthetic linear regression experiments. The left panel shows the slowly decaying-spectrum regime, where ASGD and HB are nearly overlapping while HB improves serial runtime over SGD, at essentially the same CE as SGD. The right panel shows the rapidly decaying-spectrum regime predicted by our theory: ASGD improves small-batch CE over HB/SGD, and then spends this CE advantage to reduce serial runtime as the batch size grows. Table 2 summarizes the corresponding power-law scalings.

In summary, HB preserves SGD-level CE over a larger batch-size range and uses this to improve serial runtime, but it does not improve the CE frontier itself. ASGD improves the small-batch CE frontier, but its linear-scaling window is shorter; beyond this window, larger batches buy serial-time improvements by spending some of ASGD’s CE advantage.

2 Related Work

Acceleration with Noisy Gradients.

The suboptimality of GD (Cauchy and others, 1847) for quadratic models has been well studied in literature (Nesterov, 2013). In their seminal works, Polyak (1964) and  Nesterov (1983) have proposed different variants of momentum, namely heavy ball and Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method, which improve the deterministic rate to 𝒪⁡(κ)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}). Several works have shown that for SGD with batch size 11, both HB and NAG do not improve its compute efficiency (Jain et al., 2018; Kidambi et al., 2018). Extensions to these algorithms have been studied by introducing an extra momentum buffer (Kidambi et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2024), a family of algorithms commonly refered to as accelerated SGD (Morwani et al., 2025; Ferbach et al., 2025), which provably improve the contraction at batch size 11.

Closely related to our work is the work of Lee et al. (2022), who analyze heavy-ball momentum for high-dimensional random least squares in a proportional asymptotic regime. They consider mini-batch sizes β\beta satisfying β/n→ζ>0\beta/n\to\zeta>0 as the sample size nn and feature dimension dd grow with d/nd/n fixed, and show that acceleration appears only once the batch fraction crosses a spectrum-dependent implicit conditioning ratio (ICR), a notion analogous to a critical batch fraction. For upper bounds, Liu and Belkin (2018) established upper bounds at arbitrary batch size for an algorithm named MaSS, which is schematically similar to ASGD.

ASGD Variants in Practice.

Several momentum schemes based on ASGD have been used in practice, in particular for large language model (LLM) pretraining. Morwani et al. (2025) have shown that the Schedule-Free algorithm (Defazio et al., 2024) can be rewritten as an ASGD equivalent. AdEMAMix (Pagliardini et al., 2024) uses a similar scheme, based on a fast and slow momentum buffer updated with different EMA parameters. Interestingly, Lion (Chen et al., 2023), an algorithm discovered via genetic algorithms, also interpolates between the current gradient and momentum, before applying 𝚜𝚒𝚐𝚗\mathtt{sign} on the update. Several other methods have been proposed in the literature that aggregate over more than 11 momentum buffer (Lucas et al., 2018; Ma and Yarats, 2018). DANA (Ferbach et al., 2025; Bordelon and Mori, 2026) is parametrically related to ASGD: it uses a single momentum buffer together with a direct gradient path in the parameter update, but, notably, chooses the parameters as a function of the model size and training time, rather than keeping them constant.

Nature of the bounds.

Our results are finite-dimensional, discrete-time lower bounds. For HB, the bound holds for arbitrary finite spectra; for ASGD, the stated comparison holds under the two-sided power-law spectral assumption. In both cases, the bounds hold uniformly over all stable parameter choices, including aggressive choices near the edge of stability, and only hide universal constants. Although we summarize the power-law consequences using large-dd scaling notation, these scalings come from finite-dd inequalities rather than asymptotic limits. For heavy ball, Lee et al. (2022) provide a lower bound in a proportional limit, showing that there is no acceleration in the small batch size regime.

Divergence thresholds.

The techniques used in this work to derive the lower bounds also, implicitly, characterize the edge of stability (Cohen et al., 2021; Cohen et al., 2022) conditions of the discussed algorithms. Recently, Andreyev et al. (2026) have derived stability thresholds for heavy ball and Nesterov momentum, which we also implicitly recover through the proof of Theorem 1.

4 Compute Efficiency Lower Bounds

We analyze these algorithms through the covariance dynamics of an augmented state vector ztz_{t} dependent on the distance to the optimizer wt−w⋆w_{t}-w^{\star}, and includes all variables needed to make the dynamics first-order linear in the covariance Σt=𝔼⁡[zt​zt⊤]\Sigma_{t}=\mathbb{E}[z_{t}z_{t}^{\top}]. For each method, the error covariance satisfies a linear recursion

Σt+1=𝒯⁡(Σt)\Sigma_{t+1}=\mathcal{T}(\Sigma_{t})

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a positive operator defined on the space of PSD matrices that depends on the data covariance HH, batch size BB and the algorithm hyperparameters. Since the excess risk is a linear function of Σt\Sigma_{t} (Wu et al., 2022a; Zou et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022b; Meterez et al., 2025a), the risk contraction is mainly governed by the spectral radius ρ⁡(𝒯)=maxi⁡|ti|\rho(\mathcal{T})=\max_{i}|t_{i}| where tit_{i} are the eigenvalues of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Thus, establishing lower bounds on ρ⁡(𝒯)\rho(\mathcal{T}), or equivalently upper bounds on the spectral gap s=1−ρ⁡(𝒯)s=1-\rho(\mathcal{T}) would directly imply lower bounds on the error rate for a consistent linear system. We leave the formal extension of our spectral bounds to risk bounds to future work.

We first state a general HB lower bound valid for arbitrary spectra, and then specialize it to power-law spectra to identify the critical batch-size transition. We next give an analogous bound for ASGD, showing that for power-law spectra the ASGD lower bound has a strictly better scaling than the HB lower bound in the small-batch regime and reaches the accelerated scale at a smaller batch size.

Theorem 1 (HB Compute Efficiency Lower Bound).

For any data covariance matrix HH and mini-batch size B≥1B\geq 1, β,η>0\beta,\eta>0, the optimal spectral radius of HB satisfies:

s∗​(H,B)≳ 1−min⁡{B​λmintr⁡(H),λminλmax}.\qquad s^{*}(H,B)\ \gtrsim\ 1-\,\min\!\left\{\frac{B\,\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{tr}(H)}\,,\ \sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}\right\}.\qquad

where ≳\gtrsim absorbs universal constants. In particular, the transition to the accelerated regime occurs at batch size BHBcrit=Tr⁡(H)​κλmax.B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{\Tr(H)\sqrt{\kappa}}{\lambda_{\max}}.

Theorem 1 establishes a lower bound on the optimal spectral radius of HB, which in the case of consistent linear systems governs the error rate. From the theorem, we can see that there are, in effect, 22 regimes for HB: for batch size B<BHBcritB<B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}, the algorithm cannot improve over the SGD scaling, whereas for batch size B≥BHBcritB\geq B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}} the best-achievable spectral gap is bounded above by the asymptotic contraction rate. Therefore, one can conclude that in order to minimize the number of serial steps without wasting compute, the optimal batch size to train at is BHBcritB_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}. In Corollary 1, we specialize the HB lower bound to a power law spectrum, in order to compare the rate with the ASGD bound in Section 4.2.

Corollary 1 (HB on power-law spectra).

Assume the eigenvalues of HH satisfy λi≂i−a\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a} for some a>1a>1. Then, the optimal spectral radius of HB satisfies:

s∗(H,B)≳ 1−min{Bd−a,d−a/2},s^{*}(H,B)\;\gtrsim\;1-\min\!\left\{Bd^{-a},\ d^{-a/2}\right\},

where ≳\gtrsim absorbs universal constants. In particular, the transition to the accelerated regime occurs at batch size BHBcrit≂da/2B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim d^{a/2}

We defer the full proofs to Appendix A. In the following section, we establish compute efficiency lower bounds for ASGD.

4.2 Accelerated SGD

The analysis for ASGD follows a very similar pattern as HB in Section 4.1. Note that we assume ζ>0\zeta>0 and 0<β<10<\beta<1. The ASGD update rule from Equation 3 can be written as a linear recursion in the following augmented state:

Σt+1=A​Σt​AT+η2B​[(ζ+(1−β))2​Tr⁡(H​Σt11)​Hζ⁡(ζ+1−β)​Tr⁡(H​Σt11)​Hζ⁡(ζ+1−β)​Tr⁡(H​Σt11)​Hζ2​Tr⁡(H​Σt11)​H]\displaystyle\Sigma_{t+1}=A\Sigma_{t}A^{T}+\frac{\eta^{2}}{B}\matrixquantity[\lx@physics@matrix(\zeta+ (1-\beta))^2 \Tr(H \Sigma^{11}_t)H & \zeta(\zeta+ 1 - \beta) \Tr(H \Sigma^{11}_t)H \\ \zeta(\zeta+ 1 - \beta) \Tr(H \Sigma^{11}_t)H & \zeta^2 \Tr(H \Sigma^{11}_t)H\endlx@physics@matrix]

Similarly, we will express all matrices in the eigenbasis of HH. Reusing the same notation as in Section 4.1 after rotation in the eigenbasis of HH we get Λ\Lambda and St=Q⊤​Σt​QS_{t}=Q^{\top}\Sigma_{t}Q and A=Q⊤​A~​QA=Q^{\top}\tilde{A}Q. After computing the 4th moment term using Proposition 1, the recursion becomes:

St+1=A​St​A⊤+η2B​[(ζ+(1−β))2​Tr⁡(Λ​St11)​Λζ⁡(ζ+1−β)​Tr⁡(Λ​St11)​Λζ⁡(ζ+1−β)​Tr⁡(Λ​St11)​Λζ2​Tr⁡(Λ​St11)​Λ]S_{t+1}=AS_{t}A^{\top}+\frac{\eta^{2}}{B}\begin{bmatrix}(\zeta+(1-\beta))^{2}\,\Tr(\Lambda S^{11}_{t})\,\Lambda&\zeta(\zeta+1-\beta)\,\Tr(\Lambda S^{11}_{t})\,\Lambda\\[4.0pt] \zeta(\zeta+1-\beta)\,\Tr(\Lambda S^{11}_{t})\,\Lambda&\zeta^{2}\,\Tr(\Lambda S^{11}_{t})\,\Lambda\end{bmatrix} (9)

Let 𝒯H,η,β,ζ,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B} denote the corresponding linear covariance update operator for this update rule. Then, we have the following statement.

Theorem 2 (ASGD Lower Bound under power-law spectra).

Assume the eigenvalues of HH satisfy λi≂i−a\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a} for some a>1a>1. Then the optimal spectral radius of ASGD satisfies:

s∗​(H,B)≳ 1−{B​d−a22​a−1,B≲1,Ba2​a−1​d−a22​a−1,1≲B≲d1/2,d−a/2,B≳d1/2,s^{*}(H,B)\;\gtrsim\;1-\begin{cases}B\,d^{-\frac{a^{2}}{2a-1}},&B\lesssim 1,\\[6.0pt] B^{\frac{a}{2a-1}}\,d^{-\frac{a^{2}}{2a-1}},&1\lesssim B\lesssim d^{1/2},\\[6.0pt] d^{-a/2},&B\gtrsim d^{1/2},\end{cases}

where ≳\gtrsim absorbs universal constants. In particular, the lower bound saturates at the accelerated scale at batch size BASGDcrit≂d1/2B_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim d^{1/2}.

Theorem 2 distinguishes 33 scaling regimes as a function of batch size. In the first linear regime, linearly increasing the batch size allows for a linear decrease (up to constants) in the serial steps necessary to achieve a fixed target error. After this, there is a diminishing returns regime indicating that linearly increasing the batch size gives us a sublinear decrease in the serial runtime, since for a>1a>1 the batch exponent a/(2​a−1)<1a/(2a-1)<1 (note that for large aa this term behaves roughly like B\sqrt{B}). Finally, for large batch size we reach a saturation regime, saturating the lower bound at the accelerated scale. Increasing the batch size any further would not yield any improvements in the serial runtime, and will be, instead, wasting compute.

However, note that in the power law setting, the ASGD lower bound reaches the accelerated scale at a smaller batch size than the HB lower bound. We expand upon this finding in Corollary 2.

Corollary 2 (ASGD Accelerated Regime.).

Assume the eigenvalues of HH satisfy λi≂i−a\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a} for some a>1a>1. Let BHBcritB_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}} and BASGDcritB_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}} denote the smallest batch sizes at which the HB lower bound and the ASGD lower bound, respectively, reach the optimal accelerated spectral gap Θ(d−a/2)\Theta(d^{-a/2}). Then

BHBcrit≂da/2,BASGDcrit≂d1/2.B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim d^{a/2},\qquad B_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim d^{1/2}.

Hence

BHBcritBASGDcrit≂d(a−1)/2,\frac{B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}}{B_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}}\eqsim d^{(a-1)/2},

so for every a>1a>1, the ASGD lower bound reaches the accelerated scale at a strictly smaller batch size than the HB lower bound. Equivalently, throughout the interval

d1/2≲B≲da/2,d^{1/2}\;\lesssim\;B\;\lesssim\;d^{a/2},

the ASGD lower bound has already saturated at the accelerated scale.

We defer the full proofs to Appendix B.

Compute-serial runtime tradeoff.

We now summarize the implications of the lower bounds above. Theorem 1 shows that, for arbitrary spectra, HB cannot improve over the SGD CE frontier. However, note that HB can use larger batches to reduce serial runtime, but this does not correspond to an improved compute-efficiency frontier over SGD. Beyond the HB critical batch size, the lower bound saturates at the deterministic accelerated scale.

Under power-law spectra with a>1a>1, Theorem 2 shows that ASGD has a better small-batch spectral-gap scaling than HB and that its lower bound reaches the accelerated scale at the smaller batch size BASGDcrit≍d1/2B_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\asymp d^{1/2}, as stated in Corollary 2. Thus ASGD offers a sharper compute–serial tradeoff: small batches preserve its compute-efficiency advantage, while increasing the batch size up to BASGDcritB_{\mathrm{ASGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}} converts part of this advantage into reduced serial runtime. We empirically confirm these regimes in synthetic linear-regression experiments in Section 5.

5 Experiments

We run synthetic experiments in linear regression on quadratics with power law data with a=2.0a=2.0, showing that the observed scaling is consistent with the lower bounds. We set the problem size to be D=50000D=50000 and train for N=500000N=500000, at batch sizes B∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,1024}B\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,1024\}, averaged over 5050 seeds. For both HB and ASGD we sweep over learning rate η∈{10−5,3⋅10−5,10−4,3⋅10−4,10−3,3⋅10−3,10−2,3⋅10−2,10−1,3⋅10−1,1.0,2.0,3.0,5.0,10.0}\eta\in\{10^{-5},3\cdot 10^{-5},10^{-4},3\cdot 10^{-4},10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-3},10^{-2},3\cdot 10^{-2},10^{-1},3\cdot 10^{-1},1.0,2.0,3.0,5.0,10.0\}, momentum EMA parameter β∈{0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99,0.999,0.9999}\beta\in\{0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99,0.999,0.9999\} and ASGD hyperparameter ζ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95,0.99}\zeta\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95,0.99\}, with ζ=0\zeta=0 for HB, and we plot each curve at the best set of hyperparameters. We plot the number of steps required to reach a target loss as a function of the batch size.

6 Discussion and Conclusions

In this work, we have established compute efficiency lower bounds for heavy ball momentum and accelerated SGD, as a function of the problem instance and the batch size. Specializing the problem instances to power law spectra, we have directly compared the 22 algorithms showing that there is a performance to serial runtime tradeoff: one can train with ASGD at a smaller batch size for a longer serial runtime, achieving better final loss. From a theoretical perspective, our lower bound for ASGD improves over that of (Kidambi et al., 2018), most notably due to the bound applying for any power law spectrum and not a specifically constructed problem. We believe that the techniques used in this work to derive the lower bounds can also be applied to deriving upper bounds, and we leave this derivation to future work.

Appendix A Heavy Ball Analysis

A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

The proof is a simple application of Isserlis’s theorem. Elementwise, we have that:

𝔼​[x​x⊤​Σ​x​x⊤]i​j=∑k​lΣk​l​𝔼​[xi​xk​xl​xj]=∑k​lΣk​l​(Hi​k​Hl​j+Hi​l​Hk​j+Hi​j​Hk​l)\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}\Sigma xx^{\top}]_{ij}=\sum_{kl}\Sigma_{kl}\mathbb{E}[x_{i}x_{k}x_{l}x_{j}]=\sum_{kl}\Sigma_{kl}(H_{ik}H_{lj}+H_{il}H_{kj}+H_{ij}H_{kl})

Assembling the result in matrix form gives the first part.

For v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define u:=H1/2​vu:=H^{1/2}v. Then

v⊤​H​Σ​H​v=v⊤​H1/2​(H1/2​Σ​H1/2)​H1/2​v=u⊤​H1/2​Σ​H1/2​u.v^{\top}H\Sigma Hv=v^{\top}H^{1/2}(H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2})H^{1/2}v=u^{\top}H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2}u.

Also,

Tr⁡(H​Σ)​v⊤​H​v=Tr⁡(H1/2​Σ​H1/2)​u⊤​u.\Tr(H \Sigma)\,v^{\top}Hv=\Tr(H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2})\,u^{\top}u.

Since H⪰0H\succeq 0 and Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0, we have H1/2​Σ​H1/2⪰0H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2}\succeq 0. Hence there exists an orthogonal matrix PP and a diagonal matrix D⪰0D\succeq 0 such that

H1/2​Σ​H1/2=P​D​P⊤.H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2}=PDP^{\top}.

Since D⪰0D\succeq 0, we have D⪯Tr⁡(D)​ID\preceq\Tr(D)\,I. Therefore,

u⊤​H1/2​Σ​H1/2​u=u⊤​P​D​P⊤​u≤u⊤​P​(Tr⁡(D)​I)​P⊤​u=Tr⁡(D)​u⊤​u.u^{\top}H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2}u=u^{\top}PDP^{\top}u\leq u^{\top}P(\Tr(D)I)P^{\top}u=\Tr(D)\,u^{\top}u.

Using Tr⁡(D)=Tr⁡(H1/2​Σ​H1/2)=Tr⁡(H​Σ)\Tr(D)=\Tr(H^{1/2}\Sigma H^{1/2})=\Tr(H\Sigma), we obtain

v⊤​H​Σ​H​v≤Tr⁡(H​Σ)​v⊤​H​v.v^{\top}H\Sigma Hv\leq\Tr(H\Sigma)\,v^{\top}Hv.

Since this holds for all v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, it follows that H​Σ​H⪯Tr⁡(H​Σ)​HH\Sigma H\preceq\Tr(H \Sigma)H.

A.2 Deriving the Secular Equation

So the secular equation has extra roots. But we will argue that the maximum eigenvalue of the secular equation is still associated with a per-diagonal block PSD matrix.

First, within the space of per-diagonal symmetric matrices, per-diagonal PSD matrix has the maximum eigenvalue. This follows from KT theorem, as per-diagonal PSD matrix form a total cone. Then, let’s consider the solutions of secular equation outside the symmetric space. Let MM be an eigen vector of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} which is neither symmetric nor anti-symmetric. 𝒯H,η,β,B​(M)=λ​M⟹𝒯H,η,β,B​(MT)=λ​M⊤\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}(M)=\lambda M\implies\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}(M^{T})=\lambda M^{\top}

Ms:=M+M⊤2,Ma:=M−M⊤2.M_{s}:=\frac{M+M^{\top}}{2},\qquad M_{a}:=\frac{M-M^{\top}}{2}.

Therefore, any eigenvalue carried by an eigenmatrix MM is also carried by a symmetric eigenmatrix and an anti-symmetric eigenmatrix. Also, if MM is anti-symmetric, Tr⁡(Λ​S11)=0⟹𝒯H,η,β,B​(M)=𝒯∞​(M).\mathrm{Tr(\Lambda S^{11})=0}\implies\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}(M)=\mathcal{T}_{\infty}(M). Thus, the eigenvalue of an anti-symmetric matrix for the stochastic operator coincide with the eigenvalue for the deterministic operator. In addition, note the following: (i) AA is block diagonal, (ii) give the stochastic opertor 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}, gauging at the block diagonal eigenmatrices of the determinsitc operator 𝒯∞\mathcal{T}_{\infty} suffices. For a block diagonal eigenmatrix, the eigenvalues of 𝒯∞\mathcal{T}_{\infty} are that of Ai⊗AiA_{i}\otimes A_{i}, with the eigenmatrix corresponding to the largest eigenvalue being a symmetric eigenmatrix, with rank-1 block diagonal entries of the form ui​uiTu_{i}u_{i}^{T}, where uiu_{i} represents the eigenvector of AiA_{i} corresponding to its largest eigenvalue. Thus, on the determinisitc operator 𝒯∞\mathcal{T}_{\infty}, the eigenvalue of a symmetric eigenmatrix is always greater than or equal to that of an anti-symmetric matrix. By Conjecture 3, the spectral radius for 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} is obtained by a real eigenvalue and from Lemma 2, the spectral radius of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} is lower bounded by the spectral radius for 𝒯∞\mathcal{T}_{\infty}, thus, the dominating eigenvalue of the secular equation is given by a symmetric PSD matrix.

A.3 The Zero-Noise Heavy Ball Analysis

In the deterministic setting, the Heavy-Ball iteration in Equation 6 reduces to

St+1=A​St​A⊤\displaystyle S_{t+1}=AS_{t}A^{\top} (13)

The following technical lemma governs the maximal learning rate of the deterministic Heavy–Ball algorithm.

Lemma 1 (Stability band of deterministic HB).

Assume β,η>0\beta,\eta>0. If the Heavy–Ball iteration in Equation 13 is stable (i.e. all eigenvalues of every AiA_{i} lie in the open unit disk), if and only if

β<1,0<η<2​(1+β)(1−β)​λmax.\beta<1,\qquad 0<\eta<\frac{2(1+\beta)}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}.
Proof.

Fix β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) and first consider a generic 2×22\times 2 matrix

A=[a−β10],a∈ℝ.A=\begin{bmatrix}a&-\beta\\[2.0pt] 1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad a\in\mathbb{R}.

Let r±r_{\pm} be the eigenvalues of AA, i.e. the roots of

z2−a​z+β= 0.z^{2}-az+\beta\;=\;0.

We recall the standard discrete-time stability criterion for a degree–22 polynomial. Writing this polynomial in the form

z2+p​z+q=0z^{2}+pz+q=0

with p=−ap=-a and q=βq=\beta, the Jury/Schur stability test states that the roots lie strictly inside the unit disk, |z|<1|z|<1, if and only if

|q|<1,1+p+q>0,1−p+q>0,1−q>0.|q|<1,\qquad 1+p+q>0,\qquad 1-p+q>0,\qquad 1-q>0.

(These are the degree–22 Jury conditions.)

In our case, substituting p=−ap=-a and q=βq=\beta into the above gives

|q|<1\displaystyle|q|<1 ⇔|β|<1,\displaystyle\iff|\beta|<1,
1+p+q>0\displaystyle 1+p+q>0 ⇔1−a+β>0⇔a<1+β,\displaystyle\iff 1-a+\beta>0\iff a<1+\beta,
1−p+q>0\displaystyle 1-p+q>0 ⇔1+a+β>0⇔a>−(1+β),\displaystyle\iff 1+a+\beta>0\iff a>-(1+\beta),
1−q>0\displaystyle 1-q>0 ⇔1−β>0.\displaystyle\iff 1-\beta>0.

Thus, for the matrix AA, the eigenvalues satisfy |r±|<1|r_{\pm}|<1 if and only if |β|<1|\beta|<1 and

−(1+β)<a< 1+β.-(1+\beta)\;<\;a\;<\;1+\beta.

We now apply this to the deterministic HB iteration on the quadratic. In particular, we apply these conditions to each state matrix AiA_{i}, where ai=(1+β)−η⁡(1−β)​λia_{i}=(1+\beta)-\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{i}. Stability for all ii requires

−(1+β)<ai<1+βfor allλi∈[0,λmax].-(1+\beta)<a_{i}<1+\beta\quad\text{for all}\quad\lambda_{i}\in[0,\lambda_{\max}].

The upper bound ai<1+βa_{i}<1+\beta is satisfied, since η>0\eta>0 by assumption. The lower bound must hold in particular at the largest curvature λmax\lambda_{\max}, where aia_{i} is smallest:

(1+β)−η⁡(1−β)​λmax>−(1+β).(1+\beta)-\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}\;>\;-(1+\beta).

Rearranging,

(1+β)−η(1−β)λmax>−(1+β)⟺2(1+β)>η(1−β)λmax⟺η<2​(1+β)(1−β)​λmax.(1+\beta)-\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}>-(1+\beta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2(1+\beta)>\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\eta<\frac{2(1+\beta)}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}.

Finally, stability also requires |β|<1|\beta|<1 and 1−β>01-\beta>0, which in our nonnegative-β\beta setting is exactly 0≤β<10\leq\beta<1. Combining these conditions gives the claimed deterministic HB stability band. ∎

A.4 Compute Efficiency (CE) lower bounds

Let s⁡(H,η,β,B)s(H,\eta,\beta,B) denote the spectral radius of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}:

s⁡(H,η,β,B):=ρ⁡(𝒯H,η,β,B):=max⁡{|s|:s​eigenvalue of​𝒯H,η,β,B}.s(H,\eta,\beta,B):=\rho\big(\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}\big):=\max\{\,|s|:s\ \text{eigenvalue of}\ \mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}\,\}.

As we see later on (in Lemma 3), this spectral radius is attained by a real, nonnegative eigenvalue with a PSD eigenmatrix.

We define the optimal spectral radius attainable at batch size BB as

s∗​(H,B):=infη>0,β∈[0,1)s⁡(H,η,β,B),s^{*}(H,B):=\inf_{\eta>0,\ \beta\in[0,1)}s(H,\eta,\beta,B),

and the corresponding spectral gap as 1−s∗​(H,B)1-s^{*}(H,B).

Theorem 3 (HB–SGD compute efficiency lower bound).

For any covariance matrix HH and mini-batch size B≥1B\geq 1, β,η>0\beta,\eta>0, the optimal spectral gap satisfies

s∗​(H,B)≥ 1−8​min⁡{B​λmintr⁡(H),λminλmax}.\qquad s^{*}(H,B)\ \geq\ 1-8\,\min\!\left\{\frac{B\,\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{tr}(H)}\,,\ \sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}\right\}.\qquad

A.5 Helper Lemmas

We will refer to any eigenvalue ss solving the secular equation equation 12 as an observable eigenvalue, i.e., an eigenvalue whose eigenmode has nonzero coupling to the scalar observable SwS_{w}. Recall the secular equation for the observable eigenvalue ss of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}:

1=F⁡(s):=cB​∑i=1dλi2​ϕi​(s) 1−c​λi2​ϕi​(s),c=η2​(1−β)2,1\;=\;F(s)\;:=\;\frac{c}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{\lambda_{i}^{2}\,\phi_{i}(s)}{\,1-c\,\lambda_{i}^{2}\phi_{i}(s)\,}\,,\qquad c=\eta^{2}(1-\beta)^{2}, (14)

with

ϕi​(s)=s⁡(s+β)(s−β)​(s−ri,+2)​(s−ri,−2),ri,±=ai±ai2−4​β2,ai=(1+β)−η⁡(1−β)​λi.\phi_{i}(s)=\frac{s(s+\beta)}{(s-\beta)\,(s-r_{i,+}^{2})\,(s-r_{i,-}^{2})}\,,\quad r_{i,\pm}=\frac{a_{i}\pm\sqrt{a_{i}^{2}-4\beta}}{2},\quad a_{i}=(1+\beta)-\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{i}. (15)

The poles of ϕi\phi_{i} are at s=βs=\beta and s=ri,±2s=r_{i,\pm}^{2}; for a deterministically stable HB choice, all these poles lie in (0,1)(0,1). We now formalize the intuition that adding stochastic gradient noise can only slow convergence. In particular, it cannot yield a larger spectral gap than the deterministic Heavy–Ball dynamics.

In the zero-noise case (full batch, B=∞B=\infty), the Heavy–Ball iteration on the [wt,wt−1][w_{t},w_{t-1}] state induces the deterministic covariance recursion

St+1=A​St​A⊤,S_{t+1}\;=\;AS_{t}A^{\top},

where A=blkdiag⁡(A1,…,Ad)A=\mathrm{blkdiag}(A_{1},\dots,A_{d}) is the block-diagonal state matrix in the HH-basis (with AiA_{i} as defined in Equation 7). Let

𝒯(∞)​(S):=A​S​A⊤\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}(S):=ASA^{\top} (16)

denote this deterministic (zero-noise) covariance operator.

Lemma 2 (Stochastic spectral radius dominates deterministic).

For every (η,β,B)(\eta,\beta,B) we have

ρ⁡(𝒯H,η,β,B)≥ρ⁡(𝒯(∞))=ρ​(A)2.\rho\big(\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}\big)\ \geq\ \rho\big(\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}\big)\;=\;\rho(A)^{2}.

Equivalently, the stochastic spectral gap is no larger than the deterministic gap:

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤ 1−ρ​(A)2.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\;\leq\;1-\rho(A)^{2}.

Before proving this, we record a Perron–Frobenius–type fact for the covariance operators, which follows from the Krein–Rutman theorem (Perron–Frobenius for positive operators on cones).

Corollary 3 (Perron–Frobenius for covariance maps).

Let 𝒮2​d\mathcal{S}^{2d} denote the space of real symmetric 2​d×2​d2d\times 2d matrices and let 𝒦:={S∈𝒮2​d:S⪰0}\mathcal{K}\;:=\;\{\,S\in\mathcal{S}^{2d}:S\succeq 0\,\} be the cone of positive semidefinite (PSD) matrices. Consider either of the covariance operators 𝒯∈{𝒯H,η,β,B,𝒯(∞)}\mathcal{T}\in\big\{\,\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B},\ \mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}\,\big\}. Then:

  • •

    𝒯\mathcal{T} is a positive operator on the cone 𝒦\mathcal{K}, i.e. if S⪰0S\succeq 0, then 𝒯⁡(S)⪰0\mathcal{T}(S)\succeq 0.

  • •

    The spectral radius

    ρ⁡(𝒯):=max⁡{|s|:s​eigenvalue of​𝒯}\rho(\mathcal{T}):=\max\{\,|s|:s\ \text{eigenvalue of}\ \mathcal{T}\,\}

    is attained by a real, nonnegative eigenvalue. That is, there exists S⋆∈𝒦∖{0}S_{\star}\in\mathcal{K}\setminus\{0\} and a real λ⋆≥0\lambda_{\star}\geq 0 such that

    𝒯⁡(S⋆)=λ⋆​S⋆,λ⋆=ρ⁡(𝒯).\mathcal{T}(S_{\star})=\lambda_{\star}S_{\star},\qquad\lambda_{\star}=\rho(\mathcal{T}).

In particular, each covariance operator admits a principal eigenpair (λ⋆,S⋆)(\lambda_{\star},S_{\star}) with λ⋆=ρ⁡(𝒯)\lambda_{\star}=\rho(\mathcal{T}) and S⋆⪰0S_{\star}\succeq 0.

The corollary shows that the leading asymptotic mode of the covariance dynamics can always be represented by a PSD eigenmatrix.

We now prove Lemma 2.

Proof of Lemma 2.

For brevity, write 𝒯(B):=𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}^{(B)}:=\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}. From the exact recursion and the definition of 𝒯(∞)\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)} in equation 16, we can write

𝒯(B)​(S)=𝒯(∞)​(S)+𝒩B​(S),\mathcal{T}^{(B)}(S)=\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}(S)+\mathcal{N}_{B}(S),

where the linear “noise map” 𝒩B\mathcal{N}_{B} is

𝒩B​(S):=η2​(1−β)2​[1B​Λ​Tr​(Λ​Σ11)000],S=[Σ11Σ12Σ12⊤Σ22].\mathcal{N}_{B}(S):=\eta^{2}(1-\beta)^{2}\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{1}{B}\,\Lambda\,\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda\Sigma_{11})&0\\[3.0pt] 0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad S=\begin{bmatrix}\Sigma_{11}&\Sigma_{12}\\[2.0pt] \Sigma_{12}^{\top}&\Sigma_{22}\end{bmatrix}.

If S⪰0S\succeq 0 then Σ11⪰0\Sigma_{11}\succeq 0, and both Λ​Σ11​Λ\Lambda\,\Sigma_{11}\,\Lambda and Λ​tr​(Λ​Σ11)\Lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda\Sigma_{11}) are PSD. Hence 𝒩B​(S)⪰0\mathcal{N}_{B}(S)\succeq 0, and therefore

𝒯(∞)​(S)⪯𝒯(B)​(S)for all ​S⪰0.\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}(S)\;\preceq\;\mathcal{T}^{(B)}(S)\qquad\text{for all }S\succeq 0.

Apply Corollary 3 to the deterministic operator 𝒯(∞)\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)} acting on 𝒦\mathcal{K}. There exists an eigenpair (λ∞,S∞)(\lambda_{\infty},S_{\infty}) with

S∞⪰0,S∞≠0,𝒯(∞)​(S∞)=λ∞​S∞,λ∞=ρ⁡(𝒯(∞)).S_{\infty}\succeq 0,\quad S_{\infty}\neq 0,\qquad\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}(S_{\infty})=\lambda_{\infty}S_{\infty},\qquad\lambda_{\infty}=\rho\big(\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}\big).

Since S∞⪰0S_{\infty}\succeq 0 and 𝒩B\mathcal{N}_{B} is PSD-valued on 𝒦\mathcal{K}, the domination relation implies

𝒯(B)​(S∞)=𝒯(∞)​(S∞)+𝒩B​(S∞)⪰λ∞​S∞.\mathcal{T}^{(B)}(S_{\infty})=\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}(S_{\infty})+\mathcal{N}_{B}(S_{\infty})\succeq\lambda_{\infty}S_{\infty}.

By induction,

(𝒯(B))n​(S∞)⪰λ∞n​S∞for all ​n≥1.\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}(S_{\infty})\succeq\lambda_{\infty}^{n}S_{\infty}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

Fix a matrix norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| on 𝒮2​d\mathcal{S}^{2d} that is monotone on the PSD cone: 0⪯Y⪯X0\preceq Y\preceq X implies ‖Y‖≤‖X‖\|Y\|\leq\|X\|. The spectral norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} has this property, since ‖X‖2=λmax​(X)\|X\|_{2}=\lambda_{\max}(X) for X⪰0X\succeq 0 and Y⪯XY\preceq X implies λmax​(Y)≤λmax​(X)\lambda_{\max}(Y)\leq\lambda_{\max}(X).

The induced operator norm of (𝒯(B))n(\mathcal{T}^{(B)})^{n} is

‖(𝒯(B))n‖:=supS≠0‖(𝒯(B))n​(S)‖‖S‖.\big\|\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}\big\|:=\sup_{S\neq 0}\frac{\big\|\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}(S)\big\|}{\|S\|}.

Evaluating this supremum at S=S∞S=S_{\infty} and using monotonicity on the cone,

‖(𝒯(B))n‖≥‖(𝒯(B))n​(S∞)‖‖S∞‖≥‖λ∞n​S∞‖‖S∞‖=λ∞n.\big\|\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}\big\|\;\geq\;\frac{\big\|\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}(S_{\infty})\big\|}{\|S_{\infty}\|}\;\geq\;\frac{\big\|\lambda_{\infty}^{n}S_{\infty}\big\|}{\|S_{\infty}\|}=\lambda_{\infty}^{n}.

By Gelfand’s formula,

ρ⁡(𝒯(B))=limn→∞‖(𝒯(B))n‖1/n≥limn→∞λ∞=λ∞=ρ⁡(𝒯(∞)).\rho\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\big\|\big(\mathcal{T}^{(B)}\big)^{n}\big\|^{1/n}\;\geq\;\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda_{\infty}=\lambda_{\infty}=\rho\big(\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}\big).

Finally, 𝒯(∞)\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)} acts as A⊗AA\otimes A on the vectorized state, so its eigenvalues are products λi​λj\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j} of eigenvalues of AA. Therefore

ρ⁡(𝒯(∞))=maxi,j⁡|λi​λj|=(maxi⁡|λi|)2=ρ​(A)2.\rho\big(\mathcal{T}^{(\infty)}\big)=\max_{i,j}|\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}|=\big(\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}|\big)^{2}=\rho(A)^{2}.

Combining the two inequalities yields the claimed bound. ∎

A.6 Proof

We start with a step size bound for HB–SGD.

Lemma 3 (Stability step-size cap).

Assume HB–SGD with parameters (η,β,B)(\eta,\beta,B) is stable, i.e., all eigenvalues of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} satisfy |s|≤1|s|\leq 1. Then the step size must satisfy

η≤min⁡{2​Btr⁡(H),2​(1+β)(1−β)​λmax}.\eta\;\leq\;\min\!\left\{\frac{2B}{\mathrm{tr}(H)}\,,\ \frac{2(1+\beta)}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}\right\}.
Proof.

First, let us show that stability forces

F⁡(1)≤ 1.F(1)\ \leq\ 1.

Any real ss with F⁡(s)=1F(s)=1 corresponds to an eigenvalue ss of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B}. In the stable regime, all eigenvalues of 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} satisfy |s|≤1|s|\leq 1, so in particular there can be no real eigenvalue s>1s>1. ϕi​(s)=O⁡(1/s)\phi_{i}(s)=O(1/s) implies F⁡(s)→0F(s)\to 0 as s→∞s\to\infty. Therefore, if F⁡(1)>1F(1)>1, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there exists s>1s>1 with F⁡(s)=1F(s)=1, which would correspond to an eigenvalue s>1s>1 and hence contradict stability. This proves the claim.

At s=1s=1, we can evaluate ϕi​(1)\phi_{i}(1) explicitly. Using

(1−ri,+2)​(1−ri,−2)=(1+β)2−ai2=2​(1+β)​η​(1−β)​λi−η2​(1−β)2​λi2,(1-r_{i,+}^{2})(1-r_{i,-}^{2})=(1+\beta)^{2}-a_{i}^{2}=2(1+\beta)\,\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{i}-\eta^{2}(1-\beta)^{2}\lambda_{i}^{2},

we obtain

Lemma 4 (Gap in terms of η\eta and β\beta).

For any stable HB–SGD parameters (η,β,B)(\eta,\beta,B), the spectral gap satisfies

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤min⁡{4​η​λmin,1−β}.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\;\leq\;\min\big\{4\eta\lambda_{\min},1-\beta\big\}.
Proof.

By Lemma 2, the stochastic covariance operator 𝒯H,η,β,B\mathcal{T}_{H,\eta,\beta,B} has spectral radius at least that of the deterministic (full-batch) HB operator:

where A=blkdiag⁡(A1,…,Ad)A=\mathrm{blkdiag}(A_{1},\dots,A_{d}) is the deterministic HB state matrix in the [wt,wt−1][w_{t},w_{t-1}] state. Hence

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤ 1−ρ​(A)2.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\ \leq\ 1-\rho(A)^{2}.

We first bound the gap by 1−β1-\beta. For each coordinate ii, the per–coordinate block AiA_{i} has eigenvalues ri,±r_{i,\pm} satisfying ri,+​ri,−=βr_{i,+}r_{i,-}=\beta. Thus

max⁡{|ri,+|,|ri,−|}2≥|ri,+​ri,−|=β.\max\{|r_{i,+}|,|r_{i,-}|\}^{2}\ \geq\ |r_{i,+}r_{i,-}|=\beta.

Taking a maximum over ii yields ρ​(A)2≥β\rho(A)^{2}\geq\beta, so

1−ρ​(A)2≤ 1−β.1-\rho(A)^{2}\ \leq\ 1-\beta.

Therefore

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤ 1−β.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\ \leq\ 1-\beta.

We now show 1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤4​η​λmin1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\leq 4\eta\lambda_{\min}. Let AminA_{\min} be the 2×22\times 2 HB block corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue λmin\lambda_{\min}, with eigenvalues rmin,±r_{\min,\pm} solving

z2−amin​z+β=0,amin=(1+β)−η⁡(1−β)​λmin.z^{2}-a_{\min}z+\beta=0,\qquad a_{\min}=(1+\beta)-\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\min}.

As AminA_{\min} is a block of AA, we have

ρ⁡(A)≥max⁡{|rmin,+|,|rmin,−|}.\rho(A)\ \geq\ \max\{|r_{\min,+}|,|r_{\min,-}|\}.

Hence

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤ 1−ρ​(A)2≤ 1−max⁡{|rmin,+|,|rmin,−|}2.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\ \leq\ 1-\rho(A)^{2}\ \leq\ 1-\max\{|r_{\min,+}|,|r_{\min,-}|\}^{2}.

We distinguish the real and complex cases for rmin,±r_{\min,\pm}.

For case of real roots (the overdamped case), Assume rmin,±∈ℝr_{\min,\pm}\in\mathbb{R}, which corresponds to amin2>4​βa_{\min}^{2}>4\beta. We have 1−ρ​(A)2≤(1−rmin,+2)≤2​(1−rmin,+)1-\rho(A)^{2}\leq(1-r_{\min,+}^{2})\leq 2(1-r_{\min,+}). The roots satisfy

(rmin,+−1)​(rmin,−−1)=1−(rmin,++rmin,−)+rmin,+​rmin,−=1−amin+β=η⁡(1−β)​λmin.(r_{\min,+}-1)(r_{\min,-}-1)=1-(r_{\min,+}+r_{\min,-})+r_{\min,+}r_{\min,-}=1-a_{\min}+\beta=\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\min}.

Since the roots are real and satisfy r+​r−=βr_{+}r_{-}=\beta with r−≤r+r_{-}\leq r_{+}, we must have r−≤βr_{-}\leq\sqrt{\beta}. Using that β≤1\beta\leq 1 (stability),

1−ρ​(A)2≤2​(1−rmin,+)=2​η⁡(1−β)​λmin1−r−≤2​η⁡(1−β)​λmin1−β=2​η​(1+β)​λmin≤4​η​λmin,1-\rho(A)^{2}\leq 2(1-r_{\min,+})=2\frac{\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{1-r_{-}}\leq 2\frac{\eta(1-\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{1-\sqrt{\beta}}=2\eta(1+\sqrt{\beta})\lambda_{\min}\leq 4\eta\lambda_{\min},

which completes the proof of this case.

For case of complex roots (underdamped case), assume rmin,±r_{\min,\pm} are complex conjugates, where amin2<4​βa_{\min}^{2}<4\beta. Then both have modulus β\sqrt{\beta}, so

Now we are equipped to complete the proof of Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

Fix HH and any stable HB–SGD parameters (η,β,B)(\eta,\beta,B).

Combining Lemma 4 (the step size cap) with Lemma 3 (the bound on 1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)), we obtain three simultaneous upper bounds on the same quantity 1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B):

1−s⁡(H,η,β,B)≤min⁡{4​η​λmin, 1−β}≤min⁡{8​B​λmintr⁡(H),8​(1+β)​λmin(1−β)​λmax, 1−β}.1-s(H,\eta,\beta,B)\ \leq\ \min\!\left\{4\eta\lambda_{\min},\ 1-\beta\right\}\ \leq\ \min\!\left\{\frac{8B\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{tr}(H)}\,,\ \frac{8(1+\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}\,,\ 1-\beta\right\}.

Using the definition of s∗​(H,B)s^{*}(H,B), it remains to bound:

1−s∗​(H,B)≤supβ∈[0,1)min⁡{8​B​λmintr⁡(H),8​(1+β)​λmin(1−β)​λmax, 1−β}.1-s^{*}(H,B)\ \leq\ \sup_{\beta\in[0,1)}\ \min\!\left\{\frac{8B\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{tr}(H)}\,,\ \frac{8(1+\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}\,,\ 1-\beta\right\}.

The first term inside the minimum does not depend on OPENβ)\beta), so the proof consists in bounding:

supβ∈[0,1)min⁡{8​(1+β)​λmin(1−β)​λmax, 1−β}.\sup_{\beta\in[0,1)}\ \min\!\left\{\ \frac{8(1+\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}\,,\ 1-\beta\right\}.

The first function in the min is increasing in β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), while the second is decreasing. Consequently, the sup\sup is achived at the at the crossing point β⋆\beta^{\star}, where

8​(1+β⋆)​λmin(1−β⋆)​λmax=1−β⋆⟺(1−β⋆)2=8(1+β⋆)λminλmax.\frac{8(1+\beta^{\star})\lambda_{\min}}{(1-\beta^{\star})\lambda_{\max}}=1-\beta^{\star}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(1-\beta^{\star})^{2}=8(1+\beta^{\star})\,\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}.

Hence

supβ∈[0,1)min⁡{8​(1+β)​λmin(1−β)​λmax, 1−β}=1−β⋆=8​(1+β⋆)​λminλmax=4​λminλmax,\sup_{\beta\in[0,1)}\ \min\!\left\{\ \frac{8(1+\beta)\lambda_{\min}}{(1-\beta)\lambda_{\max}}\,,\ 1-\beta\right\}=1-\beta^{\star}=\sqrt{8(1+\beta^{\star})\,\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}=4\,\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}},

using 1+β⋆≤21+\beta^{\star}\leq 2. This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 4 (HB on power-law spectra).

Assume the eigenvalues of HH satisfy λi≂i−a\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a} for some a>1a>1. Then, the optimal spectral radius of HB satisfies:

s∗(H,B)≳ 1−min{Bd−a,d−a/2},s^{*}(H,B)\;\gtrsim\;1-\min\!\left\{Bd^{-a},\ d^{-a/2}\right\},

where ≳\gtrsim absorbs universal constants. In particular, the transition to the accelerated regime occurs at batch size BHBcrit≂da/2B_{\mathrm{HB}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim d^{a/2}

Proof.

Under the power-law spectrum

λi≂i−a,λmax≂1,λmin≂d−a,a>1,\lambda_{i}\eqsim i^{-a},\qquad\lambda_{\max}\eqsim 1,\qquad\lambda_{\min}\eqsim d^{-a},\qquad a>1,

Theorem 3 gives

s∗​(H,B)≥ 1−8​min⁡{B​λmintr⁡(H),λminλmax}.s^{*}(H,B)\;\geq\;1-8\min\!\left\{\frac{B\lambda_{\min}}{\operatorname{tr}(H)},\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}\right\}.

Now,

B​λmintr⁡(H)≂B​d−a∑i=1di−a.\frac{B\lambda_{\min}}{\operatorname{tr}(H)}\;\eqsim\;\frac{B\,d^{-a}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}i^{-a}}.

Since a>1a>1, we have

∑i=1di−a≂1⟹B​λmintr⁡(H)≂B​d−a.\sum_{i=1}^{d}i^{-a}\eqsim 1\implies\frac{B\lambda_{\min}}{\operatorname{tr}(H)}\eqsim B\,d^{-a}.

Also,

λminλmax≂d−a1=d−a/2.\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}\;\eqsim\;\sqrt{\frac{d^{-a}}{1}}=d^{-a/2}.

Therefore

min{B​λmintr⁡(H),λminλmax}≂min{Bd−a,d−a/2},\min\!\left\{\frac{B\lambda_{\min}}{\operatorname{tr}(H)},\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}}\right\}\eqsim\min\!\left\{B\,d^{-a},\,d^{-a/2}\right\},
⟹s∗(H,B)≳ 1−min{Bd−a,d−a/2}.\implies s^{*}(H,B)\;\gtrsim\;1-\min\!\left\{B\,d^{-a},\,d^{-a/2}\right\}.

∎

B.1 Deterministic learning-rate stability

Lemma 5 (Deterministic ASGD stability band).

Assume η>0\eta>0. The deterministic ASGD iteration

St+1=A​St​A⊤S_{t+1}=AS_{t}A^{\top}

is stable, i.e. all eigenvalues of every AiA_{i} lie in the open unit disk, if and only if

0<η<2​(1+β)(1−β+ζ⁡(1+β))​λmax.0<\eta<\frac{2(1+\beta)}{\bigl(1-\beta+\zeta(1+\beta)\bigr)\lambda_{\max}}.
Proof.

For each coordinate ii, write

Ai=[ai−βci0],ai=(1+β)−η⁡(ζ+1−β)​λi,ci=1−η​ζ​λi.A_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}a_{i}&-\beta\\ c_{i}&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad a_{i}=(1+\beta)-\eta(\zeta+1-\beta)\lambda_{i},\qquad c_{i}=1-\eta\zeta\lambda_{i}.

Its characteristic polynomial is

r2−ai​r+β​ci=0.r^{2}-a_{i}r+\beta c_{i}=0.

Applying the degree–22 Jury criterion to

r2+p​r+q=0withp=−ai,q=β​ci,r^{2}+pr+q=0\qquad\text{with}\qquad p=-a_{i},\quad q=\beta c_{i},

the roots lie in the open unit disk if and only if

|q|<1,1+p+q>0,1−p+q>0.|q|<1,\qquad 1+p+q>0,\qquad 1-p+q>0.

The condition 1+p+q>01+p+q>0 becomes

1−ai+β​ci>0,1-a_{i}+\beta c_{i}>0,

which simplifies to

η​λi​(1−β)​(1+ζ)>0.\eta\lambda_{i}(1-\beta)(1+\zeta)>0.

This holds automatically for η>0\eta>0, λi>0\lambda_{i}>0, 0<β<10<\beta<1, and ζ>0\zeta>0.

The condition 1−p+q>01-p+q>0 becomes

B.3 Proof of the ASGD rate bound

We define the optimal ASGD spectral radius and gap at batch size BB by

s∗​(H,B):=infη>0,β∈[0,1),ζ>0s⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B),α∗​(H,B):=1−s∗​(H,B).s^{*}(H,B):=\inf_{\eta>0,\ \beta\in[0,1),\ \zeta>0}s(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B),\qquad\alpha^{*}(H,B):=1-s^{*}(H,B).

For every stable choice of (η,β,ζ)(\eta,\beta,\zeta), the deterministic dominance argument gives

α⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B)≤1−ρ​(A)2.\alpha(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B)\leq 1-\rho(A)^{2}.

Combining this with equation 24, we obtain

α⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B)≲min⁡{η​λmin​(1+ζ),(1−β)+η​β​ζ​λmin}.\alpha(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B)\lesssim\min\Bigl\{\eta\lambda_{\min}(1+\zeta),\,(1-\beta)+\eta\beta\zeta\lambda_{\min}\Bigr\}. (31)

We split into two cases.

Case 1: ζ≥1\zeta\geq 1.

In this regime, using equation 31 and equation 30,

α⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B)≲η​λmin​(1+ζ)≲1+ζζ​λmin≂d−a.\alpha(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B)\lesssim\eta\lambda_{\min}(1+\zeta)\lesssim\frac{1+\zeta}{\zeta}\lambda_{\min}\eqsim d^{-a}.

Thus the branch ζ≥1\zeta\geq 1 is at best of order d−ad^{-a}, so it cannot yield acceleration.

Case 2: 0<ζ<10<\zeta<1.

In this regime, 1+ζ≂11+\zeta\eqsim 1, so the first term in equation 31 is

η​λmin​(1+ζ)≂η​d−a.\eta\lambda_{\min}(1+\zeta)\eqsim\eta d^{-a}.

For the second term, using equation 26,

(1−β)+η​β​ζ​λmin≤(1−β)+η​ζ​d−a≲η​ζ​k−a+η​ζ​d−a≲η​ζ​k−a,(1-\beta)+\eta\beta\zeta\lambda_{\min}\leq(1-\beta)+\eta\zeta d^{-a}\lesssim\eta\zeta k^{-a}+\eta\zeta d^{-a}\lesssim\eta\zeta k^{-a},

since k≤dk\leq d implies k−a≥d−ak^{-a}\geq d^{-a}. Therefore

α⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B)≲η​min⁡{d−a,ζ​k−a}.\alpha(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B)\lesssim\eta\,\min\{d^{-a},\,\zeta k^{-a}\}. (32)

Now combine equation 32 with the two step-size caps equation 30 and Lemma 5. For every stable choice of (η,β,ζ)(\eta,\beta,\zeta) with 0<ζ<10<\zeta<1,

α⁡(H,η,β,ζ,B)≲min⁡{B​d−ak1−a+ζ,d−aζ,B​ζ​k−ak1−a+ζ,k−a}.\alpha(H,\eta,\beta,\zeta,B)\lesssim\min\left\{\frac{B\,d^{-a}}{k^{1-a}+\zeta},\,\frac{d^{-a}}{\zeta},\,\frac{B\,\zeta\,k^{-a}}{k^{1-a}+\zeta},\,k^{-a}\right\}. (33)

At this point, η\eta and β\beta have been eliminated: the right-hand side is an upper bound valid for every stable (η,β,ζ)(\eta,\beta,\zeta), and it depends only on the induced threshold kk and on ζ\zeta. Thus

α∗​(H,B)≲sup1≤k≤d, 0<ζ<1min⁡{B​d−ak1−a+ζ,d−aζ,B​ζ​k−ak1−a+ζ,k−a}.\alpha^{*}(H,B)\lesssim\sup_{1\leq k\leq d,\ 0<\zeta<1}\min\left\{\frac{B\,d^{-a}}{k^{1-a}+\zeta},\,\frac{d^{-a}}{\zeta},\,\frac{B\,\zeta\,k^{-a}}{k^{1-a}+\zeta},\,k^{-a}\right\}. (34)

We now optimize over ζ\zeta for fixed kk. Set

ζk:=(kd)a.\zeta_{k}:=\left(\frac{k}{d}\right)^{a}.

This is the crossover point where

d−a=ζ​k−a.d^{-a}=\zeta k^{-a}.

For fixed kk, define

α∗​(H,B)≤αdet∗​(H),\alpha^{*}(H,B)\leq\alpha^{*}_{\det}(H),
